title: Contextual token-skew: quant kernels and tail-latency case study
content:
Summary:

This note documents a reproducible tail-latency regression we observed in mixed-precision serving when request token distributions are heavily skewed — i.e., a small percentage of requests generate long contexts and dense attention patterns while the majority are short. The regression appears strongly correlated with kernel switchover frequency + queueing/backpressure when using AWQ/GPTQ kernels alongside our INT8 and FP8 execution paths.

Why this is interesting / new:
- Prior bench notes focused on static single-request tails (long-context throughput). This doc isolates an operational pattern we see in production: skewed token-length mix combined with bursty arrival patterns creates intermittent kernel contention that amplifies p99+ latency.
- The failure mode is not only kernel throughput differences; kernel-switching transitions (copying KV cache or switching tiling strategies) plus request coalescing logic increase queueing depth and cause cascading queue amplification under certain batch shapes.

Experiment setup (replicable):
- Hardware: 8x A100-SXM (80GB) node used as dedicated cluster. CUDA 12.2, cuBLAS/cuDNN shipped in runtime image.
- Runtime: serving-runtime commit 8c3d4f9 (branch: mixed-quant-probe).
- Models: Llama2-13B (FP16 baseline), GPTQ-13B (INT8 compiled), AWQ-13B (AWQ-INT8 variant), FP8-13B (experimental FP8 kernels).
- Config: single model routed to a single worker pool, autoscaling disabled, max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=8, dynamic_batching=true. KV cache warmup enabled.
- Traffic generator: mixed-token-client v0.3 (script attached in linked artifacts). Workload mixes: 90% short (avg 12 tokens), 10% long (avg 1024 tokens). Arrival: Poisson with mean rps=600 sustained; superimposed 1:30 bursts (2s bursts at 2x rps).
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (ms), kernel execution time per layer (sampled 1/50 requests), queueing depth time-series, batch shapes histogram, CPU thread contention (schedstats), and GPU SM occupancy traces.

Observed signals (May 02–05 runs):
- Overall median latencies across variants were comparable (FP16 baseline median ~52ms).
- p95/p99 divergence:
  - FP16 baseline: p95=140ms, p99=320ms
  - INT8 (GPTQ): p95=180ms, p99=640ms
  - AWQ (INT8-ish): p95=210ms, p99=1140ms (frequent spikes >1500ms observed)
content_extra:
- FP8 experimental: p95=160ms, p99=520ms

Notes on traces:
- Kernel switchover hotspots: when a long request arrives into a worker currently executing short-request-optimized kernel path, we see a synchronous path change that forces: (1) KV cache prefetch/swap, (2) buffer re-tiling for vector lanes, (3) different GEMM kernel selection budgets. These steps add an amortized per-switchover cost of ~18–42ms observed in traces for AWQ kernels and ~8–16ms for GPTQ kernels.
- Backpressure amplification: dynamic_batching groups short requests into a cohort; when a long request joins the cohort during the batch window, the batch shape becomes skewed. The kernel-selection code does an all-or-nothing switchover for the batch which adds the switchover cost to every short request in the same batch, producing many short requests with inflated latencies.
- Queueing contour: queue depth time-series shows sawtooth pattern; during bursts the queue grows, the percentage of batches that flip kernels increases from ~2% baseline to ~22% during bursts, correlating with the jump in p99.
- CPU contention: thread-level profiling shows the scheduler stalls increase when switchover happens due to cache-line contention on the global kernel-dispatch structure. This contributed ~6–10ms extra per switch in high load.

Hypotheses (what's causing the worst tails):
1) Kernel switchover is implemented at batch level and uses global dispatch locks for stability, causing per-batch latency cliffs when mixed request shapes coalesce.
2) AWQ kernels (current implementation) have higher one-time path-change fixed cost because they need to install quantization-specific fused ops and different tiling metadata; these costs increase nonlinearly with sequence length variance.
3) Dynamic batching policy (batch_timeout_ms and max_batch_size) when combined with skewed token-length distributions amplifies the number of mixed-shape batches and therefore the number of switchover events.

Quick reproducible test (local dev):
1) Run traffic generator with --mix 0.9/0.1 --rps 600 --burst-profile=1:30 --seed 2026
2) Enable per-layer kernel trace: KERNEL_TRACE=1 make bench-client
3) Observe batch-shape histogram: ./bin/trace-visualizer --file traces.json --metric batch-shape

Mitigations evaluated and short results:
- Mitigation A: Per-request kernel pinning (route each request to a worker pool pre-configured for the expected kernel based on estimated token-length).
  Result: p99 improved for AWQ from 1140ms -> 420ms; median unchanged. Operational downside: headroom and utilization efficiency dropped ~12% because pools sit idle on mismatched mixes.
- Mitigation B: Batch-aware switchover (defer kernel change until batch window boundary and only when >50% of batch benefits).
  Result: reduced unnecessary flips. p99 AWQ -> 720ms. Complexity: adds latency to some long requests (median of long reqs increased by ~16ms).
- Mitigation C: Fast-path microkernel for mixed batches (experimental): implement a shallow fallback kernel that can handle mixed shapes without full tiling swap; essentially low-optim throughput but low-switchover overhead.
  Result: p99 AWQ -> 360ms, but overall throughput decreased ~6%. Requires non-trivial kernel engineering.
- Mitigation D: Smart batching policy: detect skewed batch shapes during queueing and avoid coalescing long requests with short ones (e.g., stall short requests for one extra micro-window to wait for short peers).
  Result: p99 AWQ -> 380ms; added tail to some short-request percentiles but improved overall p99. Tradeoff configurable by SLO.

Action items (near term):
- (Ravi) Open a follow-on PR to make kernel selection lock-free for the dispatch table (prototype exists in branch kernel-lock-free-2026). Goal: remove global cache-line contention. Target: 2-week cycle. (JIRA-ENG-2871)
- (Diego) Implement batch-shape heuristic to avoid mixing long + short inside 8ms window. Validate with synthetic traffic. SLA must remain for throughput. (PR: #1427)
- (Sophie) Start a small perf-engineering spike for microkernel fallback design with AWQ vendor team; estimate T-shirt size and perf delta.
- Add service-level metric: "batch_mixed_shape_rate" to console and alert when >5% sustained.

Longer-term research questions:
- Can we predict request token-length reliably from prompt metadata and route earlier (client -> edge hinting)? If so, we can avoid most mixed batches with near-zero perf overhead.
- Are there kernel compilation strategies that make switchover essentially zero by keeping shared metadata structures across formats? This may require changes in kernel fusion planning and greater RAM but could be a big win.

Appendix: sample microbench numbers (single worker experiments; numbers are median / p95 / p99 in ms for end-to-end request):
- Baseline FP16: 52 / 140 / 320
- GPTQ (INT8): 58 / 180 / 640
- AWQ (current): 62 / 210 / 1140
- AWQ + Mitigation D (smart batching): 64 / 185 / 380
- FP8 experimental: 56 / 160 / 520

Notes on reproducibility and gotchas:
- GPU warm cache matters: runs with cold KV-cache show much higher variance; ensure warmup by sending 50 warmup long requests prior to measurement.
- The arrival pattern RNG seed can flip whether a high p99 spike happens early in a short run; use sustained 10–15 minute runs for stable stats.
- SM occupancy traces for AWQ showed sporadic underutilization during switchover periods — this indicates the worker sits idle while CPU performs metadata reconfiguration.

If you want to reproduce quickly, ping me (Ava) on #serving-runtime and I can hand over the traffic harness and the exact runtime image tag.

Raw trace attachments: (in linked artifacts)

Discussion notes from meeting 2026-05-07:
- Team consensus: the quickest wins are policy-level (smart batching + per-request hints) while kernel engineering (microkernel or lock-free dispatch) is medium investment with higher upside.
- SRE: want an opt-in runtime flag to prefer lower tail (cost trade). Product: wants guardrails for dedicated customers to toggle tail-vs-throughput preference.

End of note.
